name: Sam Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for taking the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a response team covering Westbank, which is the stadium, the tech park and a big stretch of student housing along the river. On a match day it's crowds and fights, on a normal Tuesday it's burglaries, car crashes and a lot of welfare checks. Between calls I'm usually the one on the laptop in the car, because I've got a habit of building little tools. Last year I made a sheet that flags addresses we keep getting called back to, and the inspector now uses it in briefings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what tires you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy solving things, whether it's a burglary pattern or a broken printer. What tires me out is the rota, four nights in a row and then trying to sleep through the day in a flat above a bakery. I live with my brother Danny, who drives buses, so between us we're never awake at the same time. I use AI tools every day, for summaries, for checking law and for my side projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest, and I'd say it with a grin. At work I'd tell people the useful bits are still useful: the report helper, the translation tool for calls in other languages. Online I'd say the hype people owe us all an apology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. My job's steady, the pay's normal, and I've got about five months saved plus a small index fund. The worst part is that the clever ideas I've got for the force would stay small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing response work and keep building my little tools on the side. I'd sit the sergeant exam next spring, because if technology isn't going to change the job, rank is how I'd move up. I'd keep putting 150 a month into the index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a tiny bit bored. Like a film that ends quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the translation tool. How much does that matter on a shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot more than people think. Westbank has students from everywhere, and last month I took a statement from a Vietnamese woman at 2am using the translation app while we waited for an interpreter. In this picture that kind of thing stays, and it's genuinely good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Danny say if you told him the AI was mostly hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say 'told you, the buses still need me'. Danny's been the sceptic in the family forever. He'd enjoy being right a bit too much.

say: I'd say I'm **a bit disappointed**, with a grin.
I'd tell colleagues the **useful bits** like translation stay useful.
think: My job is **steady**, with five months saved and a small index fund.
My ideas for the force would **stay small**.
do: Keep putting **150 a month** into the index fund.
Keep building **small tools** for the shift.
feel: **Calm** and a little **bored**, like a film that ends quietly.
S0.quote: Last month I took a statement from a Vietnamese woman at 2am using the translation app while we waited for an interpreter.
fieldNote: He is **mildly let down** by a quiet world, which is unusual.
He switches to **rank** as the way up when tech doesn't change the job.
His examples of AI are **practical**, like translation on night calls.

steps.text: Sit the sergeant exam next spring
Keep paying 150 a month into his index fund
Keep building repeat-address and summary tools for the shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version I'd want, honestly. At work I'd tell people to get ahead of it, and I'd offer to help anyone stuck. Online I'd post the stuff that actually works in a patrol car, because most of what's out there is written by people who've never sat in one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. The force would need people who understand both the street and the software, and there aren't many of us. The risk is for colleagues who won't touch it, and for civilian staff in the control room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to the new crime analysis team the moment it's advertised, probably within six months. I'd offer to run a pilot on my shift where the AI drafts the reports and we check them. I'd do a short online course in data analysis, about three months of evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. Like the job just got a new level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said colleagues who won't touch it. Who do you think of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My crewmate Greg, who's brilliant on the street and still prints his emails. If the force starts measuring people by how fast they close reports in the system, Greg looks worse on paper than he is. I'd sit with him for an hour a week if he'd let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Running a pilot means bringing the tool in yourself. Any doubts about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some. If the pilot goes well, the force might use it to cut a post, and I'd have helped. But I'd rather design the AI pilot than have it done to us by someone in an office.

I'd post **what actually works** in a patrol car.
I'd offer to help any colleague who gets **stuck** on the new systems.
think: The force would need people who know **street and software**.
Colleagues who **won't touch it** and control room staff carry the risk.
do: Apply to the **crime analysis team** within six months.
Run a **report-drafting pilot** on my shift.
Do a three-month online **data analysis course**.
feel: **Excited**, like the job just got a new level.
S1.quote: I'd rather design the AI pilot than have it done to us by someone in an office.
fieldNote: He sees **opportunity** first and names the risk to others second.
He is willing to **bring in the tool** himself, while admitting it might cut a post.
His care for a **crewmate** shows a warm side under the enthusiasm.

steps.text: Apply to the force's new crime analysis team within six months
Run a pilot where AI drafts reports and officers check them
Take a three-month online data analysis course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: this is too fast for a police force. I'd say every system that decides who gets stopped needs testing, and two years doesn't allow it. I'd also say it's coming either way, so officers had better learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it changes the maths for me. The crime analysis job I'd want is thinking work, so AGI does it in 2028. The street part buys me until about 2031, when the robots catch up. So I've got maybe five years of policing left, and I'd want to use them to land somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. In the first year I'd get a drone pilot licence through the force, because someone has to supervise the machines and the companies will pay for people who know police work. I'd push my savings from five months to nine. I'd look at jobs with firms that sell security systems to cities, where a former officer is worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way that makes me move. I'd hate sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave policing for one of those firms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the offer came in 2029, probably yes. It's not that I don't love the job. It's that I'd rather jump out of policing than be pushed at 31.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to get to nine months of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new car, for a start, I'd keep the old Fiesta. And I'd pause the index fund for a year and keep the cash instead, because shares can drop when everything's shaking. Danny would think I'd gone mad, since I'm usually the one telling him to invest.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** for a police force to test properly.
I'd also say it's coming anyway, so **officers should learn** it.
think: The **analysis job** I wanted is thinking work, gone by 2028.
Street work lasts until about **2031**, so maybe five policing years remain.
do: Get a **drone pilot licence** through the force in year one.
Raise savings from five to **nine months**.
Look at **security tech firms** that value police experience.
feel: **Anxious**, but the kind that makes him **move**.
S2.quote: I'd rather jump out of policing than be pushed at 31.
fieldNote: He works out the **thinking first, robots later** maths without prompting.
He'd **pause investing** for cash, a sharp change from his usual advice.
He plans to **leave**, not resist, which fits his adaptability.

steps.text: Get a drone pilot licence through the force this year
Pause the index fund and build nine months of savings
Apply to security tech firms that hire former officers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I said with the fast one, it needs testing, but with five years I'd say there's actually time to do that. I'd tell my inspector we should start a small team now, not in 2030. I'd write a short post about what officers should ask for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a decent run. I'd do the crime analysis job for two or three years, learn how the systems think, and then move into supervising them. Robots come around 2034, when I'm 35, and by then I'd want to be the one running the robots, not the one replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to the analysis team within the year. I'd get the drone licence in year two, once it's clearer which kit the force buys. I'd keep saving and investing at the normal rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good, alert way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talk about supervising the systems. Is that a real job yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, no. I'm guessing. But every time a big machine comes into a job, someone ends up watching it, fixing it and taking the blame when it goes wrong. I'd bet on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're the adaptive one in most rooms. Anything here that would actually scare you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the force bought one big system from a single company and nobody inside understood it. Then there's no job watching it, the company does that. That's the version where I'd get worried.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** to test properly.
I'd ask my inspector to **start a small team** now.
think: Five years is **a decent run** for analysis work, then supervising systems.
By **35** I'd want to run the robots, not be replaced.
do: Apply to the **analysis team** within the year.
Get the **drone licence** in year two, once the kit is clear.
Keep saving and **investing** at the normal rate.
feel: **Uneasy**, but alert in a good way.
S3.quote: Every time a big machine comes into a job, someone ends up watching it, fixing it and taking the blame when it goes wrong.
fieldNote: His bet is that a **supervising role** appears, and he admits it's a guess.
His real fear is **one vendor** owning the force's systems.
Five years lets him stay **inside policing** rather than leave.

steps.text: Apply to the crime analysis team within the year
Get a drone pilot licence in year two
Keep paying 150 a month into the index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this right, and I'd volunteer for whatever group the force sets up. To friends I'd say this is the good timeline. I'd say officers who start learning now will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm well placed. I'd be 37 when AGI lands and nearly 40 when robots come. That's enough time to make sergeant, do the analysis job and maybe a part-time degree in data or law. I'd worry more about Danny, honestly, because buses are driving themselves long before 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd sit the sergeant exam and keep building tools for the shift. I'd keep 150 a month going into the fund. And I'd sit down with Danny and talk him into a course, maybe bus fleet maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Mostly curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is Danny on your mind more than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Danny's whole job is driving, and driving is the first thing they're already automating. My brother Danny will tell you he's fine right up until the depot letter arrives. I'd rather nag him now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your calm view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the force cut training budgets, which happens every time money's tight. Then ten years means nothing because nobody gets taught. That's my worry, not the technology.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to **do this right**.
I'd tell friends this is **the good timeline**.
think: I'm **well placed**: sergeant, analysis work, maybe a part-time degree.
I worry more about my brother **Danny**, whose bus driving goes first.
do: Sit the **sergeant exam** in year one.
Keep **150 a month** going into the index fund.
Talk Danny into a **bus maintenance** course.
S4.quote: My brother Danny will tell you he's fine right up until the depot letter arrives.
fieldNote: His worry moves from himself to his **brother's job**.
He names **training budget cuts** as the real threat, not the technology.
Shows **confidence** that seems earned by habits, not bluster.

steps.text: Sit the sergeant exam in year one
Keep paying 150 a month into the index fund
Help brother Danny sign up for a bus maintenance course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd land on my feet, probably, but the force would be buying systems faster than anyone could check them. What would help is training paid for by the force, starting now, and a rule that every system has someone inside who understands it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets blamed when it goes wrong. Right now if I get something wrong, it's my name on the report. If a machine gets an arrest wrong, I want to know whose name goes on the report.

headlineQuote: If a machine gets an arrest wrong, I want to know whose name goes on the report.
portrait: Sam is a **27-year-old response officer** in a stadium and student district who builds small tools for his shift.
He lives with his brother Danny, a **bus driver**, and has five months saved plus an index fund.
He sees slow change as **opportunity** and plans a move to crime analysis.
With fast AGI he'd **jump** to security tech before being pushed.
His worries keep turning to **accountability** and to his brother's job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with systems bought faster than anyone can check them.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that every system has **someone inside** who understands it.
